details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You sit on the edge of the workbench, the glowrod lit in your right hand, the barred door five feet away. Wick stands a step back from it, hands at his sides, off the plank.

"Every night, you said. How many nights has it been calling?"

"Five nights."

You look down at the packed earth between your boots.

"How long ago did your people reach out to the council?"

"After Garrick didn't come back." He keeps his eyes on the door. "She sent from the long set. In her office at the Grange."

You reach for him through the Force. It comes clear and close. He is frightened, and each time the voice comes it pulls at him, and he holds against it. Under the fear, grief. The settled thing you felt in him before is still there, still leaning toward the trees. At the word council something in him shuts like a door. Resentment. And under the grief, near the surface, guilt.

"Maybe they didn't come last time. I'm here now, and I'm calling them anyway."

Wick looks at you. He says nothing.

You open the comm. The hiss comes back at your collar. His eyes go to it and stay there; he says nothing about it either.

"Varon - Varon Narik - Do you copy? I am calling from an open comms channel. Private Varon Narik - Copy?"

The hiss. You give it half a minute. Nobody answers. Down the lane, the Grange stays silent on the channel.

"Maybe no one will come. We will just have to form a tighter plan."

The channel is still open. Every word you say now goes out over it.

You tell him. That the thing out there is not his mother. That it wears voices and draws people close, and that going to it would kill him. That his mother told him to stay in to keep him from running blind at something that is not what it pretends to be. That you are not asking him to stay in: you are asking him to help you strip this place, so that when you go out you go out ready, and that when he hears that voice he has to hear through it. That if she is alive, that is how you find her.

"Can you wield a blaster?"

He breathes in, long, and lets it go.

"Okay." Then: "Rifle. For vermin. Never a blaster."

He doesn't come away from the door. He stands where he is and watches it.

Faint through the boards, from far down the rise:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

Wick goes still. He stares at the door and says nothing.

You reach for him again. This time it is very clear. Something in him has eased; he is listening. The pull toward the trees is still there, but quieter now, held against something.

"The night she went out the Grange door. Who went with her?"

"Nobody." His voice is flat. "She went on her own."

He doesn't say where she was going. He doesn't seem to know.

You clip the glowrod back on your belt, still lit, and reach back into your pack with your left hand. The crew datapad comes out cold. You press it on. Nothing: no light, no tone. You try again. The screen stays black.

You turn it over under the white light. A standard crew work slate, scuffed at the corners. One short-range link for syncing with a base unit, nothing more: no long-range housing, no transmitter. Charged or not, it could never have reached off-world. And with no charge at all, there is nothing on it to read.

You walk the length of the shed with it in your left hand. The voice calls again behind you, through the boards, the same words. At the back wall you turn the heater's dial. It ticks, and ticks, and a dull orange glow comes up behind its grille. Warmth begins, faint, against your shins.

The lockers open on their lever latches. HADDOW: coveralls, boots, gloves, and a heavy folding utility knife. PELL: the same clothes, and a hand lamp. VARRO: the same, and another folding knife. G. TOLLIVER: coveralls, boots, gloves. Nothing else.

One-handed, you clear them out. Everything goes onto the cot beside the creased blanket: two knives, the lamp, four sets of work clothes. The lockers stand open and empty.

Thirty feet away, Wick stands by the barred door, watching it. The comm hisses at your collar. The heater ticks. Far down the rise, at its own patient interval, the voice keeps calling.

details.text:
The heater ticks at your knee, its grille a dull orange, the first warmth of the night reaching your shins. The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam and throws the whole shed white, end to end. Thirty feet away, at the far end, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, his hands at his sides, his face to the plank.

You slide the dead datapad into the backpack on your back. Your left hand comes away empty. You touch the comm at your collar and the hiss there stops. The channel is closed. Nothing more goes out.

You lift a hand toward the heater.

"Heater's on. We're warm, we're lit, we're barred. We use the time."

Wick looks round at you. Then back at the door. He says nothing.

On the cot the two folding knives lie side by side on the creased blanket, heavy. You pick one up in your right hand. It is closed, and it has weight to it, a work tool, not a toy. The other stays where it is, beside the hand lamp and the coveralls.

"Come back here, Wick. Take a knife. You keep it on you from now on."

He does not turn. "In a minute."

He stays where he is.

"While you're at it, try some of these clothes on. You're going to need protection."

"Later." He says it to the door.

The second knife stays on the blanket. The coveralls stay where they lie, four sets, with the boots and the gloves.

Then, faint through the boards, from far down the rise:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words, the same way. It comes in through every gap the light goes out through.

Wick does not move. His shoulders draw up and settle. Under his breath, so low it barely crosses the thirty feet between you:

"Hear through it."

The heater ticks. The light hums. Outside, the night goes on.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. The heater ticks at your knee. Thirty feet up the shed, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, his face to the plank.

"Stay on the door if you need to. I'll bring the knife to you."

"Yeah." He says it to the door. He doesn't turn.

You put the folded knife away in a pocket of your robes. Both hands come away empty.

The coveralls lie in a heap on the creased blanket. You spread them out one by one. Heavy work cloth, a name stencilled across each back: HADDOW. PELL. VARRO. G. TOLLIVER. All four are cut for grown men. All four are stiff at the knees and the cuffs with dried clay, pale grey, that cracks and sifts onto the blanket when you bend the cloth. VARRO's breast pocket gives up a stub of yellow marking chalk. HADDOW's, a balled pair of glove liners. In PELL's hip pocket your fingers find a fold of flimsi: a stores chit. 1 x cell, hand lamp. Signed Pell. Never stamped as filled.

PELL's set is the smallest. It is still long in the leg and wide in the shoulder for a boy of sixteen. The boots are all men's boots. You take PELL's coveralls and gloves in your left hand and leave the boots where they stand.

You walk the twenty-five feet up the shed. Wick hears you come and doesn't turn. You set the coveralls and the gloves on the workbench, an arm's length from him, and say nothing.

He looks down at them. Then at you. Then back at the door. He doesn't touch them.

You walk back down the shed to the cot.

The hand lamp is a squat crew work lamp, a barrel with a lens screwed onto its end. You pick it up in your right hand and thumb the switch. It clicks. Nothing. You click it again. Nothing.

With your left hand you unclip the glowrod from your belt, still lit, cool white across the blanket. You unscrew the lamp's lens. The flat cell tips out of its well into your palm, and you set it down on the cot. The glowrod goes into the barrel in its place. It is a close fit; you turn it, ease it down, and it seats. The lens screws back down over it. Light throws out of the lamp's mouth in a beam across the back wall.

You unscrew the lens again, switch the glowrod off inside, and screw the lens back down. The lamp goes dark in your hand. You put it in a pocket of your robes. Your own light is out now. The glowpanels still hold the whole shed in white.

Fifteen feet up the shed, at the hauler's nose, the charging lead hangs coiled on its post. You lift it off and push the plug into the sled's socket. It seats.

The gauge stays dark. No light comes up on the driver's stand. Nothing shows that it is charging. The key sits in its switch, turned to off.

Faint through the boards, from far down the rise:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

Wick stands where he is, facing the door. Under his breath:

"Hear through it."

You walk the ten feet to the workbench. The coveralls lie where you left them, beside him. Above the bench the site chart hangs on its pin, flat and white under the strip light: the shaft drawn straight down under Silo Three's base, the cramped column of depths beside it, the deepest written 13.5. You go over it again, line by line. Nothing more comes out of it.

While you are still bent over it, the voice comes again. The same words. The same breath before them.

Wick does not move. "Hear through it."

You straighten up. He is five feet from you, close enough to see the muscle working in his jaw.

"Your mum, before she went. Did she take anything with her? A light, a tool?"

He doesn't answer at once. When he does, it's to the door.

"Her coat. Nothing else." A breath. "She didn't even take a light."

The heater ticks at the far end of the shed. The strip light hums. Outside, the night goes on.

"The Warden." He doesn't look round. "Everything goes through her. Cells, seed, fuel. She counts it all." A pause. "She said cells were for the winter."

He says nothing. He stays facing the door, fifteen feet from you, the knife a hard square in his pocket.

"You said that the Grange had a long range communicator? We may need to try there again before we go to Silo 3 - I need to get in touch with backup."

"In her office." Flat. "She won't let you near it."

He says nothing more.

The voice comes again. The same words, the same breath before them, far off in the dark beyond the boards.

Wick does not move. Under his breath: "Hear through it."

The heater ticks at the back of the shed. The strip light hums. Through every gap in the boards, the shed's light lies out across the gravel for anything to see.

details.text:
The strip light hums under the roof beam. The hauler sits nose to the door, dead on its stand, the key at on. Fifteen feet up the shed, Wick stands a step back from the barred door, facing the plank.

You bend to the sled again. Three minutes. You draw the plug from its socket and look in, seat it again, run the lead through your fingers from the post to the sled. The wall socket is live. The plug is home. The gauge on the driver's stand stays a dark glass eye. Whether it is the lead, the gauge or the cell, you still cannot tell.

You turn the key to off. Nothing changes.

"What did the crew do when the hauler went dead out on the lane?"

Wick doesn't turn. "It never went dead. Not that I saw."

You turn the key back to on. No light. No whine. The sled does not stir. The key sits at on in a dead machine, as it did before.

You walk up the shed, past the workbench, to the door.

As you reach him, the voice comes through the boards from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

Wick doesn't move. Under his breath: "Hear through it."

PELL's coveralls lie on the bench at your elbow, the gloves folded on top. You pick them up and hold them out.

He takes the bundle and holds it against his chest. His eyes stay on the door. He says nothing.

"Hands off the plank, Wick. You did well. Stay a step back."

A short nod.

You step into the space between him and the door. The plank is at your back now, the rough wood a hand's width behind your shoulders, the brackets either side. Wick is a step in front of you, the bundle in his arms, the light on his face.

"You did really well - I need you to put those clothes on over your outfit and sit down a moment."

He looks at you. Then he shakes the coveralls out. PELL, stencilled across the back. He steps into them over his own clothes, works his arms into the sleeves, pulls the gloves on. The legs are too long; he bends and rolls the cuffs twice over his boots. He takes the knife out of his trouser pocket and pushes it into the chest pocket of the coveralls.

"Fine."

He sits on the edge of the workbench, an arm's reach from the door, his gloved hands on his knees.

"The Warden's set is the only way off this world tonight. She'll let me near it."

He says nothing. He watches you.

You walk the thirty feet down the shed to the back wall. The heater ticks, its grille a dull orange. The lockers stand open and empty. On the creased blanket of the cot: the hand lamp's flat cell, three sets of work coveralls, four pairs of boots, three pairs of gloves.

Behind you, at the far end of the light, Wick sits on the bench in PELL's coveralls, the cuffs rolled, an arm's reach from the barred door.

details.text:
The heater ticks at your back, its grille a dull orange. At the far end of the light, thirty feet up the shed, Wick sits on the edge of the workbench in PELL's coveralls, an arm's reach from the barred door.

On the cot: the flat cell, the coveralls, the boots, the gloves. You take the cell, a dead slab no bigger than your palm, and push it into a pocket of your robes beside the lamp. Then the gloves, three pairs, stiff with old dirt at the fingertips, folded and pushed into the other pockets until the robes hang heavier on you. The coveralls and the boots you leave where they lie.

"Does the Warden keep sled cells at the Grange, or just lamp cells?"

Wick answers down the length of the shed. "Cells. I don't know what kind. She keeps them in the store room and counts them out."

You walk up the shed, past the dead hauler on its stand, to the bench.

As you reach him, the voice comes through the boards from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

His gloved hands close on his knees. Under his breath: "Hear through it."

You draw the blaster from the holster on your right hip with your left hand. It comes up into the white light, heavy and familiar.

"Those fit you better than I thought. Keep the gloves on."

"Okay."

You turn the pistol round and take it by the barrel, the grip offered to him, the muzzle toward your own wrist and the floor.

"You have the knife as a backup but if you're gonna go out there with me: I want you to feel confident that you can protect yourself. This blaster is mine, but if we survive the night I'll get you one that can be yours to keep."

He looks at it. He looks at it for a long moment, the grip a hand's width from his knee, and his hands stay where they are.

"I've never shot one."

The blaster stays in your hand.

You reach for him through the Force. It comes clear and close, as it has each time tonight. Fear, and under the fear a tiredness that goes all the way down. The pull from the rise is still there, an ache that tightens at each call, and he leans against it like a man leaning on a door. Shame, fresh and hot, as the grip hangs in front of him. And beneath all of it the thing he has kept to himself since the gate: settled, quiet, held against something, still leaning toward the trees. Under that, the guilt you felt before, close to the surface.

With your right hand you take the lamp out of your pocket. It sits dark in your palm, the glowrod seated behind its lens. The blaster is still in your left hand, held by the barrel, the grip toward him.

The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. The plank sits across its brackets an arm's length past Wick's shoulder. Outside, beyond the boards, the rise is quiet again.

details.text:
The glowpanel strip hums under the roof beam. You stand at the workbench by the door, an arm's length from Wick, the plank across its brackets five feet to your left. The lamp sits dark in your right hand. In your left, the blaster, held by the barrel, the grip a hand's width from his knee.

"That's all right. Nobody's born knowing how."

You keep it there.

"If you can shoot a rifle, a blaster isn't much different. You aim at the thing you want to shoot and you pull the trigger. You only fire if you are sure you want to shoot the thing. I believe in you. I need you to believe in you. Your fear only holds you back."

He looks at the grip. He does not move.

You say the Code to him, low and even. "There is no emotion; there is peace." Line after line, to the end. The heater ticks at the back of the shed. Wick listens with his eyes on the blaster and says nothing until you finish.

Then you show him. You turn the pistol in your left hand and point with the fingers of the hand that holds the lamp. The grip. The trigger, and the guard around it. The line along the top you sight down. The muzzle kept to the floor. The finger laid flat along the frame, outside the guard, until he means to fire. Three minutes, slow. Nothing is fired.

When you finish, he reaches out and takes it by the grip.

It sits wrong in his gloved hand at first, too big for him. He lifts it anyway, sights along the top at the back wall, at the stack of panels by the empty lockers, his finger lying flat outside the guard. He holds it there a breath. Then he lowers it, the muzzle to the floor, away from you both.

"Okay."

Your left hand is empty now. The lamp, still dark, is in your right.

The voice comes through the boards from far down the rise.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same catch on "honey". The same fall at the end.

He goes still. His eyes go to the door, to the plank, to the white light leaking through the gaps in the boards. He does not speak. The blaster stays low in his lap, the muzzle on the floor.

The rise goes quiet again.

"You've been holding something back since the gate. What is it?"

For a long moment he doesn't answer. Then, to the door, not to you:

"When the door opened I was going to go. To the trees. To her." He swallows. "I wasn't going to tell you."

You reach for him through the Force. It comes clear and close, as it has each time tonight. Fear, and the tiredness under it, all the way down. The pull from the rise is still there; he leans against it as he has all night. But something in him has steadied since his hand closed on the grip. And now, with the words out of him, a raw relief, as if he has set down something heavy. The settled thing he has carried since the gate has moved. It no longer leans toward the trees. It leans toward the door: he is waiting for it to open. Under it, the guilt you felt before has eased. Lighter, now that it is said.

"When we go to the Grange, you walk where I tell you. Every step."

He looks up at you. The blaster is low in both his gloved hands, the muzzle to the floor.

"Every step."

The strip light hums. The heater ticks. The plank sits across its brackets an arm's length past his shoulder, and beyond the boards, the rise is quiet.

The voice keeps calling from far down the rise every few minutes, the same words: 'Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path.' It can repeat words it has heard, yours included, word for word.
The shed is lit end to end; the light shows through every gap in the boards and can be seen from a long way off.
The door is barred from inside and is the only way out. The plank lifts out from inside: it takes both hands, or two people. Wick sits an arm's reach from it.
Someone pulled the feed plug out by hand. Who is unknown.
It is about two hours since the sun went down. It will not be light for about twelve hours. You have no darkvision.

plan_result.reason: Every step ran. Wick took the blaster and tried the grip; he told you he meant to go to the trees when the door opened; he said: 'Every step.'

details.position_label: standing at the workbench by the door of the dig crew's shed, at arm's length from Wick and about 5 ft from the door
